act1.label: ACT 01
act1.title: The World Indicator
act1.desc: Calculated from hundreds of data points. No algorithm, no AI model — pure code, real data.
act1.howText: Weighted average of 5 categories: Environment (25%), Society (25%), Economy (20%), Progress (20%), Momentum (10%). Each category is normalized from dozens of indicators to 0–100.
act2.label: ACT 02 — ENVIRONMENT
act2.title: The Planet Breathes
act2.desc: Temperature, CO2, air, ice, forests, renewables — the vital signs of our Earth.
act2.tempDesc: Each stripe = one year. Blue = cooler, Red = warmer than the average (1951–1980).
act2.co2Explain: Parts per million in the atmosphere. Before industrialization: ~280 ppm. Highest level in 800,000 years.
act2.tempExplain: Deviation from average (1951–1980). The Paris 1.5°C target is nearly reached.
act2.arcticExplain: Ice loss equals roughly the area of India.
act2.forestExplain: Share of land area covered by forest. ~10M hectares lost per year.
act2.renewableExplain: Share of global electricity generation. Growing exponentially thanks to solar & wind.
act2.airDesc: AQI: 0–50 good, 51–100 moderate, 101–150 unhealthy for sensitive groups, 150+ unhealthy
act2.weatherDesc: Real-time data from 8 metropolises via Open-Meteo
act3.label: ACT 05 — SOCIETY
act3.title: We the People
act3.desc: {popBillion} billion. Conflicts, displacement, freedom, health — how we are doing.
act3.conflictMapDesc: Size = intensity. Red = war, Orange = conflict, Yellow = unrest
act3.refugeeSource: Source: UNHCR {currentYear} — More than ever in history
act3.freedomDesc: 195 countries rated by political rights & civil liberties
act3.freedomDecline: {freedomStreak}th consecutive year of decline — Freedom House {currentYear}
act3.infraExplain: Billions now have access to basic services — historically unique.
act4.label: ACT 06 — ECONOMY
act4.title: The Engine
act4.desc: Wealth, poverty, inequality, trade — the numbers behind the system.
act4.wealthDesc: The richest 1% owns more than the bottom half of humanity combined.
act4.giniExplain: 0 = perfect equality, 100 = maximum inequality. Country values from the World Bank.
act4.tradeExplain: Trade as % of GDP. Declining since 2008 due to protectionism.
act5.label: ACT 07 — PROGRESS
act5.title: The Curve
act5.desc: Science, technology, education — progress is exponential.
act5.githubExplain: Open source drives innovation. Developers worldwide solve problems together.
act5.literacyGap: Gender gap is closing — but still {gap}% difference.
act6.label: ACT 08 — REAL-TIME
act6.title: Real-Time Pulse
act6.desc: Live data from around the world — updated every 6 hours from dozens of APIs.
act6.newsDesc: UN, WHO, BBC, Al Jazeera, Guardian, DW, NASA, ReliefWeb etc.
act7.label: ACT 09 — MOMENTUM
act7.question: Is it getting better — or worse?
act7.desc: Not where we stand — but where we are heading.
act7.method: Methodology: Comparing the last 3 years with the 3 years before for each indicator.
act8.label: ACT 10 — CRISES
act8.title: The Crisis Map
act8.desc: Climate, conflicts, hunger, natural disasters — and hope.
act8.infoText: Reality is complex. There are crises and progress — simultaneously, everywhere. The question is not if, but how fast we respond.
act9.label: ACT 11 — SCENARIOS
act9.title: Three Futures
act9.desc: Illustrative scenarios to 2050 — not a forecast. They show how the World Index could develop under three assumptions.
act9.bauItems: Warming of +2.1 °C by 2050|Extreme poverty: about 420 M people|Internet use at 82 %|Biodiversity: −50 % by 2050
act9.worstItems: Warming of +3.5 °C by 2050|Extreme poverty: about 900 M people|Migration: about 500 M people|Ecosystem collapse in key regions
act9.bestItems: Warming stabilised at +1.8 °C|Extreme poverty eliminated by 2040|100 % renewable energy by 2050|Universal access to education by 2035
act10.label: ACT 12 — TRANSPARENCY
act10.title: Data Sources & Transparency
act10.desc: Every data point verifiable. Every source linked. Open source.
act10.methodText: No AI. Just code and data. All calculations open-source and reproducible.
act10.methodNote: The World Indicator is based on weighted normalized sub-scores (0–100).
act11.label: ACT 13 — ACT NOW
act11.question:
You've seen the data.
What can YOU do?
act11.localDesc: Vote. Community projects. Shape local politics.
act11.digitalDesc: Open source. Data projects. Share knowledge.
epilog.message:
The data updates every 6 hours.
Come back — and see if something has changed.

detail.co2.title: CO2 in the Atmosphere
detail.co2.explanation: CO2 is the most important greenhouse gas. It is primarily produced by burning fossil fuels and amplifies the natural greenhouse effect that warms the Earth.
detail.co2.explanation2: Concentration is now higher than at any point in the last 800,000 years. Even if all emissions stopped immediately, the CO2 already released would influence the climate for centuries.
detail.co2.comparison: 280 ppm pre-industrial vs. {current} ppm today -- the highest level in 800,000 years.
detail.temperature.title: Global Temperature
detail.temperature.tp_coral_detail: Tropical coral reefs face mass bleaching at >1.0°C
detail.temperature.tp_greenland_detail: Sustained warming above 1.5°C triggers long-term melt
detail.temperature.tp_boreal_detail: Northern forests shift from carbon sink to source
detail.temperature.tp_amazon_detail: Combination of warming and deforestation threatens collapse
detail.temperature.tp_permafrost_detail: Thawing releases trapped methane and CO2
detail.temperature.tp_amoc_detail: Slowdown disrupts European climate and monsoons
detail.temperature.tp_eais_detail: Largest ice mass, potential 50m+ sea level rise
detail.temperature.tp_arcticwinter_detai: Complete loss of winter ice cover
detail.temperature.explanation: Global average temperature has risen by about 1.3°C since the pre-industrial era. The warming is caused by greenhouse gases and is accelerating.
detail.temperature.comparison: The Paris 1.5°C target is nearly reached. At the current rate, 2°C will be exceeded in the 2040s.
detail.earthquakes.title: Earthquakes Worldwide
detail.earthquakes.explanation: The Earth is tectonically active. Over 500,000 earthquakes are detected annually, of which about 100,000 are felt. Strong quakes of magnitude 7+ occur on average 15 times per year.
detail.earthquakes.comparison: Most earthquakes occur along the Pacific Ring of Fire, where tectonic plates collide.
detail.population.title: World Population
detail.population.explanation: The world population is growing, but more slowly than before. The peak is expected around 2086 at about 10.4 billion. After that, it could decline for the first time in history.
detail.population.comparison: In just 65 years, the world population tripled -- from 2.5B (1960) to 8.1B (2025).
detail.population.explainP1: The world population is growing — but slower than ever. The fertility rate has dropped from 5.0 to 2.3 children per woman since the 1960s. A decline is expected for the first time from 2086 onwards.
detail.population.explainP2: The population pyramid shows this shift: In 1960, the base dominated (many children, few elderly). By 2026, the shape is cylindrical — aging has begun. By 2050, the top will be wider than the base.
detail.population.explainP3: Urbanization is a megatrend: For the first time, the majority of humanity lives in cities. By 2050, 68% will be urban — with enormous challenges for infrastructure, housing, and the environment.
detail.conflicts.title: Conflicts & Wars
detail.conflicts.explanation: The number of armed conflicts has risen sharply since 2010. More people are currently displaced than ever before in history.
detail.conflicts.comparison: Despite rising conflict numbers, per-capita war deaths are declining long-term. Conflicts are becoming more asymmetric and primarily affect civilians.
detail.biodiversity.title: Biodiversity
detail.biodiversity.explanation: The Living Planet Index tracks the average change in population sizes of 5,230 species since 1970. A 73% decline does not mean 73% of animals are gone, but that the average population size has shrunk by 73%.
detail.biodiversity.comparison: The current extinction rate is 100-1000x above the natural background. Scientists refer to this as the sixth mass extinction.
detail.airquality.title: Air Quality
detail.airquality.explanation: The Air Quality Index (AQI) combines multiple pollutant measurements into a single number. Values below 50 are considered good, above 150 unhealthy. WHO limits are stricter than most national standards.
detail.airquality.comparison: Air pollution causes 4.2 million premature deaths worldwide annually. South Asia and Africa are most affected.
detail.forests.title: Forests
detail.forests.explanation: Forests cover 31% of Earth's land area and absorb 2.6 billion tonnes of CO2 annually. Despite reforestation efforts, net loss continues -- mainly from conversion to agricultural land.
detail.forests.comparison: Since 1990, the world has lost 178 million hectares of forest -- an area larger than Libya.
detail.renewables.title: Renewable Energy
detail.renewables.heroLabel: Renewables in the global power mix
detail.renewables.explanation: Renewable energy reached 30% of the global electricity mix for the first time in 2024. Solar is the fastest growing energy source -- installed capacity has tripled since 2018.
detail.renewables.comparison: Iceland, Norway, and Brazil generate over 80% of their electricity from renewables. Germany is at 46%.
detail.health.title: Health
detail.health.explanation: Global life expectancy has risen from 47 to 73 years since 1950. The greatest gains came from vaccinations, clean water, and reduced child mortality. Yet vast gaps remain: Japan reaches 84 years, the Central African Republic just 54.
detail.health.comparison: Countries that spend more on health tend to have higher life expectancy -- but the relationship is not linear. The US spends the most per capita but ranks only 40th globally.
detail.freedom.title: Freedom
detail.freedom.trendDesc: Since 2006, the global Freedom House score has declined every year -- the longest continuous slide on record. Authoritarian trends are accelerating worldwide.
detail.freedom.explanation: The Freedom House Score measures political rights and civil liberties in 195 countries on a 0-100 scale. Since 2006, global scores have declined -- 18 consecutive years. Authoritarian regimes increasingly undermine press freedom, assembly rights, and fair elections.
detail.freedom.comparison: Scandinavian countries lead with scores above 95. China, North Korea, and Eritrea score below 10. The steepest declines since 2015 are in Myanmar, Afghanistan, and Nicaragua.
detail.inequality.title: Inequality
detail.inequality.explanation: The Gini Index measures inequality on a scale from 0 (perfect equality) to 100 (one person owns everything). Globally it is about 38.5 -- but wealth inequality is far more extreme than income inequality. The richest 1% owns 45% of global wealth.
detail.inequality.comparison: South Africa has the highest Gini index (63), followed by Namibia and Suriname. Nordic countries score below 30. In the past 30 years, inequality between countries has decreased, but within many countries it has risen.
detail.poverty.title: Poverty
detail.poverty.explanation: Extreme poverty -- less than $2.15 per day -- has fallen from 43% to 10% since 1990. This is the greatest poverty reduction in human history. Yet around 700 million people still live in extreme poverty, mainly in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia.
detail.poverty.comparison: Sub-Saharan Africa has the highest poverty rate at 35%, but South Asia has the most affected in absolute terms. China has lifted over 800 million people out of poverty since 1990.
detail.poverty.sourcePIP: World Bank PIP (Poverty and Inequality Platform)
detail.poverty.middleEast: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan
detail.currencies.title: Currencies
detail.currencies.explanation: Exchange rates reflect the relative strength of economies. The US dollar remains the global reserve currency -- over 88% of all foreign exchange transactions involve the dollar. Currency stability is critical for trade, investment, and price stability.
detail.currencies.comparison: The Swiss franc is considered the strongest stable currency, while the Turkish lira and Argentine peso have lost massive value in recent years. Hyperinflation in Venezuela has made the bolivar practically worthless.
detail.science.title: Science
detail.science.explanation: Scientific output is growing exponentially. arXiv alone publishes over 1,800 preprints daily. Artificial intelligence is the fastest-growing research field and overtook all other categories in 2024.
detail.science.comparison: The number of scientific publications has more than tripled since 2000. China has surpassed the US in total publications, while the US leads in citations.
detail.internet.title: Internet
detail.internet.explanation: Over 5.4 billion people use the internet -- 67% of the world population. Growth is primarily driven by mobile devices in developing countries. Africa and South Asia have the greatest potential for further expansion.
detail.internet.comparison: Nordic countries achieve over 98% internet penetration, while parts of Africa remain below 20%. The digital divide remains one of the greatest challenges for global equality.
detail.space.title: Space
detail.space.explanation: The ISS orbits Earth at about 408 km altitude at 27,600 km/h -- one orbit every 90 minutes. It has been continuously crewed since 2000. Meanwhile, over 13,000 active satellites are in orbit.
detail.space.comparison: SpaceX alone conducted over 90 rocket launches in 2024. The total number of active satellites has tripled since 2019, mainly due to Starlink constellations.
detail.weather.title: World Weather
detail.weather.explanation: Real-time data from 24 global metropolises. Weather impacts agriculture, health, and the economy. Extreme weather events are increasing due to climate change -- heatwaves, storms, and floods are becoming more frequent and intense.
detail.weather.comparison: The number of extreme weather events has quintupled since 1980. Heatwaves kill more people annually than any other natural disaster.
detail.solar.title: Solar Activity
detail.solar.explanation: The Sun follows an approximately 11-year activity cycle. During the maximum, sunspots, solar flares, and coronal mass ejections increase. These affect satellite electronics, power grids, and create auroras. Cycle 25 reaches its maximum in 2024-2026.
detail.solar.comparison: The current Cycle 25 is stronger than expected but significantly weaker than the historical record of Cycle 19 (285 sunspots, 1958).
detail.crypto_sentiment.title: Crypto Sentiment
detail.crypto_sentiment.explanation: The Crypto Fear & Greed Index measures market sentiment based on volatility, volume, social media, and dominance. Extreme fear can signal buying opportunities, while extreme greed warns of overheating.
detail.crypto_sentiment.comparison: Historically, periods of extreme fear (<20) are often followed by recovery. Extreme greed (>80) has preceded corrections multiple times.
detail.momentum_detail.title: World Momentum
detail.momentum_detail.heroLabel: of {n} time series are improving (3-year average)
detail.momentum_detail.explanation: World Momentum shows how many key global indicators are improving, declining, or remaining stable. It is based on trend analyses over the last 5-10 years across 20 key indicators in 4 categories.
detail.momentum_detail.comparison: Currently more indicators are improving than declining -- but progress is unevenly distributed between environment (weak) and technology (strong).
detail.hunger.title: World Hunger
detail.hunger.explanation: Approximately 735 million people worldwide go hungry -- nearly one in ten. The causes are complex: conflicts, climate change, economic shocks, and inequality. Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia are most severely affected.
detail.hunger.comparison: The share of undernourished people dropped from 13.2% (2000) to 8.5% (2023), but absolute numbers have risen again since 2015. The zero hunger goal for 2030 will be clearly missed.
detail.disasters.title: Natural Disasters
detail.disasters.explanation: The number of reported natural disasters has more than tripled since 1980. Main drivers: better recording and climate change. Floods and storms account for over 80% of weather-related disasters.
detail.disasters.comparison: Economic damages from natural disasters exceeded $300 billion in 2024. Developing countries bear disproportionate costs despite lower CO2 emissions.
act12.label: ACT 03 — BIODIVERSITY
act12.title: The Silence of Species
act12.desc: Extinction, endangered species, the sixth mass extinction.
act12.extinctionExplain: Current extinction rate is 100-1,000x above the natural background rate.
act12.endangeredExplain: Listed as threatened on the IUCN Red List.
act13.label: ACT 04 — OCEANS
act13.title: The Oceans
act13.desc: SST anomaly, acidification, plastic — the health of our seas.
act13.sstExplain: Sea surface temperature deviation. Corals bleach above +1C.
act13.plasticExplain: Estimated total. 8-12 million tonnes are added annually.
detail.extinction.title: Species Extinction
detail.extinction.heroExplain: Factor above the natural background rate (IPBES).
detail.extinction.currentExplain: Today's extinction rate surpasses all previous mass extinctions -- driven by habitat loss, climate change, overexploitation, and invasive species.
detail.extinction.sources: IPBES Global Assessment, IUCN Red List
detail.endangered.title: Endangered Species
detail.endangered.heroExplain: Listed as threatened on the IUCN Red List.
detail.ocean_temp.title: Sea Surface Temperature
detail.ocean_temp.heroExplain: Sea surface temperature deviation from long-term average.
detail.ocean_temp.coralExplain: Degree Heating Weeks (DHW) measure cumulative ocean heat stress. Coral bleaching begins at 4 DHW — widespread mortality occurs above 8 DHW. Thresholds are based on NOAA Coral Reef Watch.
detail.ocean_temp.sources: NOAA Climate at a Glance, Coral Reef Watch
detail.ocean_ph.title: Ocean Acidification
detail.ocean_ph.acidExplain: Each 0.1 pH decrease means 26% more acidity. Shellfish, corals, and plankton can no longer form their calcium shells.
detail.ocean_plastic.title: Ocean Plastic
detail.ocean_plastic.heroExplain: Estimated cumulative plastic mass in the world's oceans.
detail.ocean_temp.explainP1: SST anomaly measures how much ocean surface temperature deviates from the historical average. Positive anomalies indicate warming seas.
detail.ocean_temp.explainP2: Rising ocean temperatures cause coral bleaching, disrupt marine food chains, intensify hurricanes, and contribute to sea level rise through thermal expansion.
detail.ocean_temp.explainP3: The ocean absorbs over 90% of excess heat from greenhouse gas emissions, making it a critical indicator of global climate change.
detail.ocean_plastic.dailyDesc: {amount} kg of plastic enter the ocean every day.
detail.ocean_plastic.explanationP1: About 80% of ocean plastic originates from land-based sources, transported primarily through rivers. The remaining 20% comes from maritime activities including fishing, shipping, and offshore platforms.
detail.ocean_plastic.explanationP2: Large plastic items break down into microplastics (< 5mm) through UV radiation and wave action, but never fully biodegrade. These microplastics enter the marine food chain.
detail.ocean_plastic.explanationP3: By 2050, the ocean could contain more plastic than fish by weight if current trends continue.
detail.ocean_ph.explainP1: Ocean acidification is a direct consequence of CO₂ absorption by seawater. Since industrialization, the ocean has become 30% more acidic.
detail.ocean_ph.explainP2: pH is a logarithmic scale -- each 0.1 step means 26% more acidity. This is catastrophic for marine organisms.
detail.ocean_ph.explainP3: Shellfish, corals, and plankton build shells from calcium carbonate. In acidic water, these structures dissolve or fail to form.
detail.ocean_ph.compPreIndustrialDesc: Natural balance before industrial CO₂ emissions.
detail.ocean_ph.compCurrentDesc: pH has dropped 0.17 units. Marine organisms are showing stress.
detail.ocean_ph.compProjectedDesc: If emissions don't decrease, pH may drop 0.5 units by 2100.
detail.extinction.bigFiveDesc: The Five Great Mass Extinctions shaped life on Earth. Each event wiped out 75-96% of marine species.
detail.extinction.currentHoloceneCause: Human activity: habitat loss, climate change, pollution
detail.extinction.rateComparisonDesc: Background extinction is the natural rate. Current rates are 100-1000x faster.
detail.extinction.timeline.contextNote: Species loss is dramatically accelerating. What took millions of years in the past now happens in decades.
detail.endangered.categoriesDesc: The IUCN Red List categorizes species by extinction risk. The darker the color, the more threatened.
detail.endangered.assessedNote: Only a fraction of Earth's species have been formally assessed. The IUCN Red List is the most comprehensive assessment, but most species remain unknown to science.
detail.endangered.explanationP1: Biodiversity loss is accelerating globally. Critically endangered species face the highest risk of extinction in the wild.
detail.endangered.explanationP2: Habitat destruction, climate change, overhunting, and pollution are the primary drivers of species extinction.
detail.endangered.explanationP3: We are experiencing a mass extinction event, with species disappearing 100-1,000 times faster than natural rates.
